opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's a really important distinction, and it's one that a lot of organizations get wrong.

Exploratory research is about questions where you don't know the answer, and you don't even know if there *is* a good answer within a reasonable time frame. The horizon is long, maybe several years, and the success criterion isn't a product metric. It's whether you've learned something, whether you've opened a new direction that other people can build on. That kind of work needs freedom. You can't put it on a quarterly roadmap. If you tell researchers "you need to ship something in six months," they will pick safe problems, incremental problems, and you'll never get the breakthroughs.

It also needs openness. You publish, you release code, you engage with the broader community, because progress in this field comes from many people building on each other's ideas. Nobody has a monopoly on good ideas. Research done in secret tends to go slower.

Turning a promising result into a product is a completely different activity. Now you know roughly what works, and the question becomes: can we make it reliable, efficient, scalable, safe, and useful to actual people? That's engineering, and it's very hard engineering. A lot of things that look great in a paper fall apart when they meet real data, real latency constraints, real users. So you need different people, different incentives, and different ways of measuring success.

The mistake is to mix the two too much. If research becomes too tightly coupled to product, it gets pulled toward short-term goals and stops being research. If it's too disconnected, the good ideas never make it out. So what you want is a separation of missions but a good interface between them, people who can carry ideas across, product teams who pay attention to what's coming out of research, and researchers who are curious about what problems actually matter.

And I'd say the history of the field shows this. Things like convolutional nets, self-supervised learning, transformers: they came out of exploratory work that nobody could have scheduled. Then it took years of engineering to make them into products that billions of people use. Both parts are essential, but they run on different clocks.

r001.rationale: The candidate contrasts exploratory research with turning a promising result into a product, describing the latter as a different activity that requires engineering.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the way I think about it, these are really two very different activities, and you have to be careful not to confuse them, because the confusion is where organizations get into trouble.

Research, real exploratory research, is about asking questions where you don't know the answer, and frankly where you don't even know if the question is well posed. The time horizon is long, the probability of success for any given project is low, and the output is knowledge. It's a paper, it's an idea, it's a demonstration that something is possible or, just as usefully, that something doesn't work. When I set up FAIR at Meta, the principle was that researchers publish, they collaborate with the outside world, and they are not evaluated on whether their work ends up in a product next quarter. If you evaluate researchers that way, they stop taking risks, and then you don't get research anymore, you get incremental engineering with a fancy name.

Now, turning a result into a product is a completely different kind of hard. It is not less difficult, it is differently difficult. You have to make it work reliably, not just on the benchmark. You have to make it cheap, you have to make it fast, you have to make it work for people who are not going to read the paper. And you have to integrate it with everything around it. Most of the ideas that come out of research are never going to make that transition, and that's fine. The ones that do often look quite different by the time they ship. Convolutional networks in the late eighties and the systems that actually read checks for banks in the nineties were connected, but there was a lot of work in between that was not research, it was engineering, and it was done by people with different skills and a different mindset.

So the distinction I draw is really about what question you are answering. If the question is "is this possible, and what is the principle behind it," that's research. If the question is "how do we make this work for ten million people at acceptable cost," that's product. And the mistake is to ask one group to do both at once, or to pretend that the second thing is the first thing because it uses the same tools. You need both, and you need a path between them, but the path should be people and ideas moving across, not research being told what to discover.

r001.rationale: It distinguishes exploratory research from making a result reliable, affordable, fast, and integrated for product use, explicitly describing that work as engineering.

astra-6.text:
Those are different activities, and they need different ways of being managed. In exploratory research, you’re asking a question whose answer you don’t know. You may have an intuition that a particular approach will work, but you can’t promise that it will work, and certainly not by a particular date. If the outcome were predictable, it wouldn’t really be research.

Turning a result into a product means working toward a much more concrete objective. You have to make the system reliable, efficient, affordable, and useful. A demonstration that works under favorable conditions is a long way from something people can depend on. That requires a lot of engineering, and sometimes it exposes problems that require new research.

So the two activities should interact, but you shouldn’t judge them by the same criteria. If every research project has to justify itself with a product launch in six months, you will mostly get incremental improvements. You need room to pursue ideas that might fail, or that might become useful much later.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes exploratory research from product development and says turning a result into a dependable product requires substantial engineering.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they require different ways of working. In exploratory research, you’re asking a question whose answer you don’t know, and often you don’t even know whether you’re asking the right question. You have to allow people to try ideas that may fail. If you require them to explain in advance exactly what product will come out of it and on what schedule, you’re limiting the kind of research they can do.

Once you have a result that looks promising, there’s a different set of questions: Can you make it reliable? Can you make it efficient? Does it solve a problem that people actually have? A demonstration is not a product. There’s a lot of engineering, experimentation, and sometimes more research between the two.

The two activities should communicate, of course. Practical problems can inspire very interesting research. But you shouldn’t manage exploratory research as if it were product development. The uncertainty is the reason you’re doing research in the first place.

r001.rationale: The candidate distinguishes exploratory research from the work after a result looks promising, describing reliability, efficiency, and problem fit as questions involving engineering and experimentation on the path to a product.
